newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-Former Peruvian rebels fall on hard times.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Former Peruvian rebels fall on hard times.

text.p: As "Commander Tarzan," he led a column of 120 Marxist rebels in raids, ambushes and firefights across jungle-covered mountains and Amazon streams during the toughest years of Peru's guerrilla wars.

Now Javier Vela lives with his wife and 3-year-old daughter in a one-room, dirt-floored adobe hut outside this steamy tropical town -- poor, jobless and staring at a bleak future. "We're basically abandoned, forgotten," he said, sitting on the edge of the family's bed, his daughter beside him assembling a child's puzzle of a barnyard scene. "We're living in a state of total crisis."

Vela is not alone. About 1,000 "repentant" Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels live in poverty and legal limbo years after they agreed to lay down arms in exchange for jobs, protection and immunity from prosecution. Thanks to Peru's byzantine judicial system, Vela and scores of other former rebels face a constant threat of arrest despite agreeing years ago to the so-called Repentance Law.

President Alberto Fujimori decreed the law at the height of guerrilla conflicts in 1992 in a bid to curb spiraling violence and weaken the pro-Cuban MRTA and larger Maoist Shining Path groups. It worked. Before the law expired on Oct. 31, 1995, thousands of leftist rebels swapped armed struggle for promises of jobs, protection and freedom from prosecution.

Although it also resulted in the arrest of hundreds of innocent Peruvians based on coerced testimony, the law has been credited with helping to stem Peru's seemingly endless cycle of political violence. But local church, human rights and legal experts in Tarapoto said the government has failed to live up to its promises.
A TIME BOMB WAITING TO EXPLODE

They warned that the combination of persecution and economic frustration felt by "repentants" is an explosive one. "This is a time bomb waiting to go off," said one expert on the region's history of guerrilla- and drug-related violence.

"The current situation of the repentants is worrisome. Underline the word 'worrisome,'" said Humberto Rodriguez Macedo, a psychologist who helped scores of rebels turn themselves in between 1992 and 1995. He said the government has failed to grant economic aid, jobs or new identities to former rebels and many former MRTA members face prison because the record of their "repentance" often is not included in cases still pending against them.

"They say 'When are they going to leave us alone?'" Rodriguez said, adding that by the time courts clear up the confusion the "repentants" could spend months or years in prison on terrorism or treason charges.
Pro-government lawmakers, some of whom said they did not recall that the law provided for officials to help "repentants" land jobs, acknowledge there have been problems.

"The problem is very complex," Congressman Genaro Colchado Arllano of Fujimori's Change 90 party said. "The government is making an effort to resolve these problems through social programmes but it can't do it from one day to the next."

The "repentants" have had even more to worry about since Dec. 17, when about 20 MRTA rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima and seized hundreds of hostages to demand the release of some 460 imprisoned comrades.

The hostage takers, led by rebel chief Nestor Cerpa, continue to hold 72 diplomats, politicians and business leaders, including a brother of President Alberto Fujimori, two cabinet ministers and Japan's envoy to Lima.

The prospect of a mass release of MRTA rebels is not a welcome one for former guerrillas. "They may seek revenge against us because they consider us traitors," said a former rebel leader who went by the nom de guerre Antonio.

The hostage crisis, followed across Peru, has been watched especially closely in Tarapoto and the rest of San Martin department, some 385 miles (620 km) north of Lima. This lush region of mountainous jungle, swollen Amazon tributaries and coca fields was for years the MRTA's main stronghold and a rich source of drug dollars to keep the movement running. MRTA slogans can still be seen on walls in poor areas and rumours of rebel columns returning to the bush crop up frequently.

Still, former rebels like Antonio, who led his column of more than 200 guerrillas out of the jungle in 1993, do not see the MRTA re-establishing itself in San Martin, and few are inclined to take up arms again.
"Any revolution I make will be within my family," said Antonio, who now drives one of the motorcycle taxis typical of the region and works part-time repairing electric appliances.
"I don't want anything to do with violence anymore," Vela said. "The people are tired of violence. What I want now is what is best for my daughter. What I need most is a job."
